title: Build a Production-Ready REST API with Node.js and Express
description: Beyond the hello-world tutorial: project structure, validation, error handling, authentication, and testing patterns for an Express API you'd actually deploy.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: Most Express tutorials stop at `app.get('/hello')` and leave you to discover everything else in production at 2 AM. This guide covers the parts that make an API production-ready: structure that survives growth, input validation, consistent errors, authentication, and tests — the unglamorous work that determines whether your API is reliable.

sections.heading: Project Setup
Structure: Routes, Controllers, Services
sections.body:
Don't put business logic in route handlers. A three-layer split keeps things testable:

``` src/ routes/ # URL wiring only: router.get('/', controller.list) controllers/ # request/response handling: parse input, call service, format output services/ # business logic: database calls, rules, computations middleware/ # auth, validation, error handling ```

Routes map URLs to controllers. Controllers translate HTTP into service calls and service results into HTTP. Services contain the actual logic and know nothing about HTTP. When you need to change how something works, you know exactly which layer to open.

sections.heading: Input Validation: Never Trust the Client
Consistent Error Handling
Authentication with JWT
Pagination, Filtering, and Sensible Defaults
sections.body:
Any endpoint returning a list needs pagination from day one. Offset-based (`?page=2&limit=20`) is simple and fine for most cases; cursor-based is better for large or frequently-changing datasets. Cap the page size server-side — a client requesting `limit=1000000` should get your maximum, not your database.

Return a consistent envelope so clients can rely on the shape:

```json { "data": [ ... ], "pagination": { "page": 2, "limit": 20, "total": 341 } } ```

sections.heading: Rate Limiting and Security Headers
sections.body:
`express-rate-limit` takes five minutes to add and stops the trivial abuse: brute-force login attempts, scrapers hammering list endpoints. Set stricter limits on auth routes than on public reads. Helmet sets sensible HTTP security headers with one line. Neither replaces real security review, but both close doors that are otherwise wide open.

Also: CORS. If your API serves a browser frontend on a different origin, configure `cors` with an explicit origin list — not `*` — when credentials or tokens are involved.

sections.heading: Testing What Matters
sections.body:
You don't need 100% coverage; you need tests on the paths that break in production:

Validation tests — send malformed bodies and assert 400s with useful messages. Auth tests — missing token, bad token, expired token, and a valid token hitting a protected route. Happy-path integration tests — spin up the app against a test database and walk through create/read/update/delete.

Supertest plus a test runner (Vitest or Node's built-in runner) covers this well. Run tests in CI on every push — an API without CI-tested deploys is a incident waiting for a schedule.

sections.heading: Logging and Observability
sections.body: Log structured JSON (a request ID, method, path, status, duration) rather than free-text strings — your future self grepping logs at midnight will be grateful. In production, ship logs to a collector instead of stdout files. Add the `/health` endpoint from the start and a `/ready` endpoint if startup involves async initialization (database connections) that load balancers should wait for.

sections.heading: Deployment Checklist
sections.body:
Environment variables set on the host, not in the repo. `NODE_ENV=production` (Express changes behavior: less verbose errors, view caching). Process manager or container restart policy — Node processes crash; plan for it. Database connection pooling sized for your host's limits. Backups tested by restoring, not by assuming.

An Express API doesn't need to be complex to be production-ready. It needs validation at the boundary, consistent errors, authentication done carefully, tests on the critical paths, and logs you can actually read. Get those right and the framework mostly stays out of your way.
